name: Raspberry Pi OS
summary: Official operating system for Raspberry Pi single-board computers, derived from Debian GNU/Linux and optimised for ARM processors with the PIXEL graphical interface under Wayland/Labwc and the raspi-config tool.
license: Open Source (free Debian licences with proprietary Broadcom firmware)

content.introduction: Raspberry Pi OS (formerly known as Raspbian) is the official operating system specially designed and optimised for the range of Raspberry Pi single-board computers (SBC). Developed and maintained by Raspberry Pi Ltd and the free software community, it is the reference distribution for learning computing, electronics prototyping, teaching digital sciences and industrial embedded deployments based on ARM boards.
content.what_is_it: Technically, Raspberry Pi OS is directly derived from the stable versions of the Debian GNU/Linux distribution. It combines the vast package software library of Debian with a custom Linux kernel compiled for Broadcom processors (BCM2835 to BCM2712 SoCs), graphics drivers adapted for the VideoCore chips, and a set of system tools developed specifically to use the input/output pins (GPIO) and the hardware interfaces of the boards.
content.origin_and_history:
Raspbian, on which the 32-bit Raspberry Pi OS images rest, is an unofficial port of Debian Wheezy armhf compiled with "hard float" settings adapted to the ARMv6 processor of the first boards. The Raspbian project attributes this work to Mike Thompson (`mpthompson`) and Peter Green (`plugwash`), states that the initial build of more than 35,000 packages was completed in June 2012, and specifies that it is not affiliated with the Raspberry Pi Foundation.

On 28 May 2020, the foundation renamed its images: the 32-bit version became "Raspberry Pi OS", presented as the new name of Raspbian, while a 64-bit beta version was published from the Debian arm64 port. The 64-bit version left beta on 2 February 2022. The two builds remain distinct: the 32-bit one relies on Raspbian, the 64-bit one on Debian.
content.architectures_and_editions: The system is distributed in two complementary hardware architectures: a 32-bit variant (`armhf`) ensuring full backwards compatibility with all board models since the very first Raspberry Pi 1 and the Pi Zero (ARMv6 and ARMv7 processors), and a 64-bit variant (`aarch64` / ARM64) fully exploiting the memory and 64-bit instructions of recent models (Raspberry Pi 3, 4, 5 and Zero 2 W). Three official editions are made available: the "Lite" edition, without a graphical server for server and lightweight embedded uses, the "Desktop" edition, offering the complete desktop environment, and the "Desktop with recommended software" edition, including development environments (Thonny, Scratch) and the LibreOffice office suite.
content.pixel_desktop_and_wayland_transition: The official graphical environment of Raspberry Pi OS, called PIXEL (Pi Executive Engineering LXDE), offers a sober, intuitive desktop that is particularly frugal in RAM. Historically based on the X11 server and the Openbox window manager, the graphical environment has carried out a major transition to the modern Wayland protocol. Initially powered by the Wayfire 3D compositor in the Bookworm branch, the desktop has adopted by default the lightweight stacking compositor Labwc (Lab Wayland Compositor) and the display management tool `raindrop`, bringing increased fluidity, optimal responsiveness on touch screens and backwards compatibility with older hardware boards through Xwayland.
content.hardware_integration_and_raspi_config: One of the distinctive traits of Raspberry Pi OS lies in its dedicated hardware administration tooling. The console-mode and graphical utility `raspi-config` makes it simple to configure the electronic communication buses (I2C, SPI, UART, CSI camera interface, DSI display, 1-Wire bus), adjust partitioning, manage the GPU shared memory and switch between display backends without manually modifying low-level configuration files (`config.txt`). Installation of the system is automated by the official Raspberry Pi Imager utility, making it possible to write the image to a microSD card, USB key or NVMe SSD while pre-configuring the Wi-Fi wireless network, the user account and the SSH keys.
content.package_ecosystem_and_maintenance_lifecy: Raspberry Pi OS benefits from the logistic richness of the Debian APT repositories (more than 69,000 packages available) supplemented by a dedicated repository hosted by Raspberry Pi for specific hardware and software components. The maintenance cycle closely follows that of the stable major versions of Debian (published every two years). In accordance with recent Debian standards, the Python development environment requires the isolation of software dependencies installed by `pip` within virtual environments (`venv`), thus guaranteeing the integrity and long-term stability of the preinstalled system tools.
content.debian_release_names: Debian code names serve as version markers: the current version of Raspberry Pi OS is based on Debian Trixie, the previous one on Debian Bookworm. Because the calendar is offset, one and the same Debian version number can correspond to several Raspberry Pi OS releases, and the two systems share neither the date nor the number of their major versions.
content.installation_and_major_upgrades: Installation goes through Raspberry Pi Imager, available for Windows, macOS and Linux, or through writing a downloaded disk image. The documentation specifies that an in-place upgrade to a new major version must not be carried out: a recent image must be reinstalled, after backing up important files, the installation overwriting the card.
content.package_management_and_firmware: APT is the default package manager, used on the command line (apt-cache, apt install) as well as through the Add / Remove Software graphical tool. The firmware is supplied by the raspi-firmware package, reinstallable to return to the last stable version if a pre-release update causes a problem. The documentation reserves rpi-update for testing and development.
content.security_and_hardening_defaults:
Several security settings are documented as default values. The SSH server is disabled on a fresh installation and can be enabled from the Control Centre, `raspi-config` or an `ssh` file placed on the boot partition. `sudo` commands require the account password, a setting enabled during the initial configuration.

Verified boot, or secure boot, is an option founded on a chain of trust: the public key of the boot ROM is inscribed in the silicon, the user generates a 2048-bit RSA key pair whose fingerprint is stored in OTP memory, then the EEPROM bootloader verifies the `boot.sig` signature of the `boot.img` image before launching the kernel. If the verification fails, the bootloader moves to the next boot mode instead of executing the unverified code. Root encryption, enabled by the same provisioning tool, uses a device-specific secret kept in OTP, which the `initramfs` reads to unlock the file system.

The documentation devotes separate pages to UFW, described as the recommended firewall and left disabled until it is configured, to Fail2Ban, installed by `sudo apt install fail2ban`, and to account management. It specifies that only the most recent major version receives all the security fixes and refers to the security advisories, the CVE reports and an SBOM supplied for each edition.
advantages: Perfect hardware and software optimisation for the whole range of Raspberry Pi single-board computers (from the Pi 1 to the Pi 5).
Remarkable stability inherited directly from the proven Debian GNU/Linux foundation.
Extremely light PIXEL desktop environment, fluid and modernised under Wayland and the Labwc compositor.
Dedicated hardware configuration tools (`raspi-config`, Raspberry Pi Imager) facilitating access to the electronic interfaces (GPIO, I2C, SPI).
Huge user community, exhaustive official technical documentation and countless educational tutorials.
Availability of 32-bit and 64-bit editions suited both to learning projects and to autonomous embedded servers (Lite edition).
disadvantages: System closely coupled to the hardware architecture of the Broadcom processors of Raspberry Pi boards (inapplicable on a standard x86-64 PC without emulation).
Mandatory presence of proprietary firmware (closed binary VideoCore GPU firmwares) required for the initial boot of the board.
Consumer microSD memory cards can show sensitivity to wear in case of frequent intensive writes (although booting from a USB or NVMe SSD is supported).
3D graphics and multimedia performance dependent on the hardware capabilities of the integrated SoC, limited on older models or the Zero series.
Non-expandable RAM constraints inherent to the all-in-one design of Raspberry Pi boards.
who_is_it_for: Pupils, teachers, students and trainers discovering computer programming, robotics and digital sciences.
Makers, electronics technicians and hobbyists developing connected objects (IoT), controllers and measurement stations using the GPIO pins.
Users of lightweight home servers seeking to deploy network services (Pi-hole DNS server, Home Assistant home automation, print server).
Industrial companies and design offices designing embedded control or dynamic display systems based on Compute Module modules.
who_is_it_not_for: Users looking for an operating system for their traditional desktop computer or their x86-64 laptop.
Professionals requiring a workstation for heavy computing, high-resolution video editing or demanding 3D games.
Free software purists refusing any proprietary binary firmware component (strictly free systems such as Trisquel or Debian free being then preferred).
Heavy virtualisation infrastructures of data centres requiring multiprocessor x86 hypervisors.
content.verdict: Raspberry Pi OS is the official operating system of Raspberry Pi single-board nano-computers. Based on Debian and on a Wayland/Labwc graphics stack, it targets education, electronics prototyping and embedded computing.

components.name: Debian
components.note: Base system: "Raspberry Pi OS is based on the Debian Linux distribution and supports over 69,000 Debian packages."; the same page adds that the latest version "is based on Debian Trixie" and that "Releases happen roughly once every two years." (documentation/asciidoc/computers/os/rpi-os-introduction.adoc, github.com/raspberrypi/documentation).

relations.name: Debian

relations.name: DietPi
relations.note: Minimalist and highly optimised alternative distribution designed specifically for single-board computers such as the Raspberry Pi.

relations.name: Ubuntu
relations.note: Linux distribution offering official images preconfigured for Raspberry Pi 4 and 5 with the GNOME desktop.

relations.name: Nura
relations.note: Linux distribution oriented towards mobility and ARM hardware sharing the use of Wayland and touch interfaces.
